title: Beliefs & Foundations
description: A question bank on foundational Islamic belief, with explanations and primary-text references.
difficultyMethod: Editorial classification; not calibrated from learner response data. Advanced means greater reasoning depth within this subject, not a scholarly qualification.

review.referenceCheck: Primary-text references checked during preparation; this is not independent scholarly approval.

selectionHints.unknownResponse: Handle I am not sure as a UI action, not as a fifth answer option.

questions.question: In Surah Al-Fatihah, whom do Muslims declare that they worship and ask for help?

options.text: Allah
The angels
The prophets
Their ancestors

questions.explanation: Al-Fatihah 1:5 directs worship and the plea for help to Allah. This is a foundational expression of devotion to Him.

questions.question: What does Surah Al-Ikhlas affirm about Allah?

options.text: He shares His rule with other gods.
He is One.
He belongs to a family of gods.
He was created by another being.

questions.explanation: Al-Ikhlas 112:1 affirms Allah's oneness. The surah also rejects offspring and any equal to Him.

questions.question: According to Quran 39:62, who is the Creator of all things?

options.text: Jibril
The first human being
Allah
The universe itself

questions.explanation: Az-Zumar 39:62 identifies Allah as the Creator of all things and the One who oversees them.

questions.question: According to Quran 6:59, which statement about Allah's knowledge is correct?

options.text: He knows only events that people report.
He knows public actions but not hidden things.
He learns about events after they happen.
Nothing, even a falling leaf, is outside His knowledge.

questions.explanation: Al-An'am 6:59 describes Allah's knowledge of the unseen and of even a falling leaf. His knowledge is not dependent on human observation.

questions.question: Which divine quality is expressed by the names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim in Al-Fatihah?

options.text: Mercy
Ancestry
Human weakness
Dependence on others

questions.explanation: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim describe Allah's mercy. English renderings vary, but both names relate to mercy.

questions.question: How does Quran 66:6 describe the angels mentioned in that verse?

options.text: They independently decide whom to worship.
They obey Allah's commands.
They require humans to worship them.
They regularly reject Allah's commands.

questions.explanation: At-Tahrim 66:6 describes these angels as carrying out Allah's commands without disobedience.

questions.question: Which angel is named in Quran 2:97 as bringing the revelation to the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission?

options.text: Mikail (Michael)
Malik
Jibril (Gabriel)
Harut

questions.explanation: Al-Baqarah 2:97 names Jibril as bringing the revelation to the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission.

questions.question: Which belief concerning revelation is taught in Quran 4:136?

options.text: Belief only in books written by later historians.
Belief that revelation began after Muhammad's death.
Belief that no prophet received revelation.
Belief in the revelation sent to Muhammad and the scripture revealed before him.

questions.explanation: An-Nisa 4:136 calls for belief in Allah, His Messenger, the Book sent to him and the scripture revealed before him.

questions.question: In Quran 87:19, whose scriptures are mentioned alongside those of Ibrahim (Abraham)?

options.text: Musa (Moses)
Yunus (Jonah)
Sulayman (Solomon)
Yahya (John)

questions.explanation: Al-A'la 87:19 names the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa.

questions.question: Which revelation does Quran 5:46 say was given to Isa (Jesus)?

options.text: The Zabur (Psalms)
The Injil (Gospel)
The Quran
The scriptures of Ibrahim

questions.explanation: Al-Ma'idah 5:46 states that Allah gave Isa the Injil, containing guidance and light.

questions.question: Which prophet is named in Quran 4:163 as receiving the Zabur (Psalms)?

options.text: Ishaq (Isaac)
Yusuf (Joseph)
Dawud (David)
Harun (Aaron)

questions.explanation: An-Nisa 4:163 specifically mentions the Zabur being given to Dawud.

questions.question: Quran 47:2 refers to revelation sent down to which prophet?

options.text: Musa (Moses)
Ibrahim (Abraham)
Nuh (Noah)
Muhammad

questions.explanation: Muhammad 47:2 refers to what was revealed to Muhammad and identifies it as truth from his Lord.

questions.question: According to Quran 16:36, what central message did messengers bring to their communities?

options.text: Worship Allah and avoid false objects of worship.
Give religious authority only to wealthy families.
Worship each messenger alongside Allah.
Replace accountability with tribal loyalty.

questions.explanation: An-Nahl 16:36 describes messengers calling people to worship Allah and avoid false objects of worship.

questions.question: How does Quran 33:40 describe Muhammad in relation to prophethood?

options.text: The first of all prophets
The seal of the prophets
A prophet whose message was only for his household
A prophet who received no revelation

questions.explanation: Al-Ahzab 33:40 describes Muhammad as Allah's Messenger and the seal of the prophets.

questions.question: In Quran 18:110, how is the Prophet instructed to describe himself?

options.text: An angel who appears human
A divine being who needs no revelation
A human being who receives revelation
A person who knows everything independently

questions.explanation: Al-Kahf 18:110 combines the Prophet's humanity with the distinctive fact that he receives revelation.

questions.question: In the Hadith of Jibril, which future reality is explicitly included in the description of iman?

options.text: A date chosen by each community
An endless worldly life for every person
The abolition of all accountability
The Last Day

questions.explanation: The Prophet includes belief in the Last Day when explaining iman in the Hadith of Jibril.

questions.question: What does Quran 22:7 affirm about those in their graves?

options.text: Allah will raise them.
They will never be raised.
Only those remembered by others will be raised.
Their return depends on their family's wealth.

questions.explanation: Al-Hajj 22:7 affirms the coming of the Hour and Allah's resurrection of those in the graves.

questions.question: What do Quran 99:7-8 teach about very small deeds?

options.text: Only deeds witnessed by a crowd matter.
Even a tiny amount of good or evil will be seen.
Small acts are automatically excluded from accountability.
Good deeds count only if they are expensive.

questions.explanation: Az-Zalzalah 99:7-8 emphasizes accountability even for very small amounts of good and evil.

questions.question: Which description of the reward for believers who do righteous deeds appears in Quran 4:57?

options.text: A further life without any judgment
A reward determined only by family name
Gardens beneath which rivers flow
The ability to decide everyone's final fate

questions.explanation: An-Nisa 4:57 describes gardens beneath which rivers flow as a reward for believers who do righteous deeds.

questions.question: What warning does Quran 4:56 describe?

options.text: The absence of any consequences for rejecting revelation
A punishment decided by a person's neighbours
The cancellation of all judgment after death
Punishment in the Fire for those who reject Allah's signs

questions.explanation: An-Nisa 4:56 warns of the Fire for those who reject Allah's signs. The question concerns the verse's warning, not a judgment about a particular individual.

questions.question: Which statement agrees with Quran 54:49 about divine decree?

options.text: Allah created everything according to a measure or decree.
Events occur outside Allah's knowledge and power.
Human planning removes Allah's authority.
Divine decree applies only to natural objects.

questions.explanation: Al-Qamar 54:49 states that everything was created according to a measure or decree.

questions.question: Which list matches the six matters of faith named in the Hadith of Jibril?

options.text: Prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, trade and family
Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day and divine decree
Angels, stars, ancestors, rulers, dreams and wealth
Books, mosques, languages, countries, customs and history

questions.explanation: The hadith identifies these six matters when defining iman. They are commonly taught as the six articles of faith.

questions.question: Which list contains the five pillars described in Sahih al-Bukhari 8?

options.text: Prayer, trade, marriage, travel and study
Fasting, family customs, dreams, charity and poetry
Testimony of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting Ramadan and Hajj
Pilgrimage, ancestry, citizenship, wealth and leadership

questions.explanation: The hadith names the testimony of faith, prayer, zakat, Hajj and fasting Ramadan. The order of the final two in a list does not change the five pillars.

questions.question: Which meaning correctly expresses the testimony of faith mentioned in Sahih al-Bukhari 8?

options.text: Allah and His messengers are equally entitled to worship.
Muhammad created the world and owns its judgment.
Belonging to a Muslim family replaces belief in Allah.
None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and Muhammad is His Messenger.

questions.explanation: The testimony affirms worship of Allah alone and Muhammad's status as His Messenger.

questions.question: In the Hadith of Jibril, which concept is described as worshipping Allah with awareness that He sees you?

options.text: Ihsan
Zakat
Hajj
Inheritance

questions.explanation: The hadith explains ihsan through excellence in worship and awareness of Allah's observation.

questions.question: According to Sahih al-Bukhari 1, what is central to the reward of an action?

options.text: The number of people watching it
The intention behind it
The social status of its performer
The language in which it is discussed

questions.explanation: The hadith connects deeds and their reward to intentions. A visible action alone does not reveal the intention behind it.

questions.question: What response to wrongdoing is encouraged by Quran 39:53-54?

options.text: Despair because forgiveness is always impossible.
Hide the wrongdoing and refuse to change.
Hope in Allah's mercy and return to Him.
Assume repentance is unnecessary because actions do not matter.

questions.explanation: These verses combine reassurance about Allah's mercy with a call to return and submit to Him.

questions.question: What does Quran 2:186 encourage a person to do?

options.text: Wait until a community leader can hear every prayer.
Limit supplication to requests made in public.
Treat supplication as a substitute for believing in Allah.
Call upon Allah.

questions.explanation: Al-Baqarah 2:186 describes Allah as near and responding to the caller. It also calls people to respond to Him and believe in Him.

questions.question: According to Quran 49:13, what distinguishes the most honoured people in Allah's sight?

options.text: Taqwa: being mindful of Allah
The size of their family
The amount of property they inherit
The popularity of their nationality

questions.explanation: Al-Hujurat 49:13 identifies taqwa, rather than ancestry or social status, as the criterion of honour before Allah.

questions.question: What is Luqman warning his son against in Quran 31:13?

options.text: Learning a useful trade
Associating partners with Allah
Travelling to another city
Caring for relatives

questions.explanation: Luqman's advice warns against associating partners with Allah and describes it as a tremendous wrong.

questions.question: Someone accepts one prophet but rejects another prophet whom Allah sent. Which teaching in Quran 2:285 challenges this approach?

options.text: Belief in a prophet depends on that prophet's nationality.
Only messengers with large followings need to be accepted.
Believers accept all of Allah's messengers.
Accepting one messenger permits rejection of the rest.

questions.explanation: The verse describes believers affirming Allah's messengers without rejecting some of them. This concerns acceptance of their messengership.

questions.question: According to Quran 7:56, which attitude should accompany calling upon Allah?

options.text: Complete confidence that no action has consequences
Despair that excludes any hope of mercy
Concern only for how others judge the supplication
Both fear and hope

questions.explanation: Al-A'raf 7:56 joins fear and hope in supplication. Neither careless complacency nor hopelessness captures that balance.

questions.question: A student says, 'If my result is decreed, there is no reason to prepare.' Which response best follows Sahih Muslim 2664?

options.text: Pursue what benefits you, seek Allah's help and do not give up.
Stop preparing because effort cannot be part of Allah's decree.
Prepare only if you can guarantee the result beforehand.
Rely entirely on preparation and reject the need for Allah's help.

questions.explanation: The hadith joins beneficial effort with seeking Allah's help. Belief in decree is not presented as a reason for helpless inaction.

questions.question: A person has consulted others and reached a decision. What does Quran 3:159 then instruct?

options.text: Wait until every uncertainty disappears.
Place trust in Allah.
Treat consultation as a guarantee of success.
Assume that advice makes trust in Allah unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Ali 'Imran 3:159 brings consultation, decision and reliance on Allah together. Trust is compatible with thoughtful action.

questions.question: A person says, 'Allah is merciful, so I do not need to turn away from wrongdoing.' What is missing from this reading of Quran 39:53-54?

options.text: A requirement to become wealthy before seeking forgiveness.
A rule that mercy applies only to people who never sinned.
The accompanying instruction to return and submit to Allah.
A promise that every action has identical consequences.

questions.explanation: The reassurance in 39:53 is followed by the call to return and submit in 39:54. The passage encourages repentance rather than indifference.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects Quran 35:15?

options.text: Allah needs people's worship to remain powerful.
Only poor people depend on Allah.
Human achievement makes a person independent of Allah.
People need Allah, while Allah is free of need.

questions.explanation: Fatir 35:15 describes humanity as dependent on Allah and Allah as free of need and worthy of praise.

questions.question: Someone believes Allah can hear a supplication only after another person forwards it. Which part of Quran 2:186 corrects this claim?

options.text: Allah describes Himself as near and responding to the caller.
Allah makes every request depend on the caller's social rank.
Allah limits hearing to one language.
Allah requires a public gathering before a person may call upon Him.

questions.explanation: The verse addresses the relationship between Allah and the person calling upon Him. It does not make His hearing dependent on a human messenger carrying the request.

questions.question: Why would worshipping angels conflict with Quran 21:26-27?

options.text: The verses describe angels as independent creators.
The verses describe angels as honoured servants who act by Allah's command.
The verses assign each angel a separate divine kingdom.
The verses say angels receive worship instead of Allah.

questions.explanation: Al-Anbiya 21:26-27 rejects attributing offspring to Allah and describes honoured servants who obey His command. Their honour does not make them gods.

questions.question: A person receives a blessing and recognizes it as a reason to thank Allah. Which teaching supports this response?

options.text: Quran 14:7 says gratitude is needed only during hardship.
Quran 14:7 limits gratitude to financial gifts.
Quran 14:7 links gratitude with an increase in blessings.
Quran 14:7 makes gratitude a reason to neglect other duties.

questions.explanation: Ibrahim 14:7 associates gratitude with increase. Thankfulness recognizes the blessing rather than treating it as proof of personal superiority.

questions.question: How does Quran 49:13 explain the existence of peoples and tribes?

options.text: So that one ancestry automatically deserves greater honour.
So that people can avoid all contact with other communities.
So that nationality replaces accountability to Allah.
So that people may know one another.

questions.explanation: The verse connects human diversity with mutual recognition and then identifies taqwa as the criterion of honour before Allah.

questions.question: Which description of righteousness best matches Quran 2:177?

options.text: Faith joined with generosity, worship, keeping promises and patience
A public religious identity without responsibility toward others
Correctly facing a direction while disregarding conduct
Wealth and reputation regardless of belief or behaviour

questions.explanation: Al-Baqarah 2:177 describes righteousness through both belief and practical responsibilities. It is not reduced to an outward symbol.

questions.question: A person knowingly chooses wrongdoing because a friend encouraged it. Which principle in Quran 6:164 still applies?

options.text: The friend's encouragement automatically removes all responsibility.
Each person remains accountable for their own deeds.
Responsibility belongs only to the oldest person present.
A person's community name cancels individual accountability.

questions.explanation: Al-An'am 6:164 states that each person earns consequences for themselves and that no bearer bears another's burden. Encouragement does not itself erase personal responsibility.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates the belief in the unseen described in Quran 2:3, read alongside Quran 2:285?

options.text: Accepting every rumour because its subject cannot be seen
Treating every dream as a binding revelation
Accepting the existence of Allah's angels on the basis of revelation
Believing that anything unobservable must be imaginary

questions.explanation: The Quran commends belief in the unseen and explicitly includes angels among the matters of faith. This is not a rule to accept every unsupported unseen claim.

questions.question: Quran 5:110 repeatedly connects Isa's miracles with whose permission?

options.text: The permission of the people watching
The permission of a ruler
Isa's independent divine authority
Allah's permission

questions.explanation: Al-Ma'idah 5:110 repeatedly attributes the occurrence of Isa's miracles to Allah's permission. Miracles do not establish independence from Allah.

questions.question: Someone says, 'Wealth always proves Allah's approval, and limited provision always proves His rejection.' What does Quran 89:15-17 challenge?

options.text: The assumption that material circumstances alone establish a person's standing with Allah.
The idea that people can experience different material circumstances.
The need to take responsibility for how wealth is used.
The fact that wealth and hardship can be tests.

questions.explanation: Al-Fajr describes both abundance and restricted provision as tests and rejects the simplistic conclusions people draw from them.

questions.question: In the Hadith of Jibril, Islam and iman receive different answers. Which explanation best preserves that distinction in this narration?

options.text: Islam is explained through six beliefs, and iman through five forms of worship.
Islam is explained through the five pillars, and iman through the six matters of belief.
Islam concerns only ancestry, and iman concerns only citizenship.
Islam and iman are presented as unrelated religions.

questions.explanation: This question concerns how the two terms are explained in this particular narration. It does not imply that belief and practice are unrelated.

questions.question: Someone thinks worship can be careless whenever other people are absent. Which reasoning best applies the hadith's description of ihsan?

options.text: Worship is meaningful only when someone can praise it.
The absence of people removes the need for sincerity.
Allah sees the worshipper even when no human observer is present.
Ihsan requires physically seeing Allah before beginning worship.

questions.explanation: The hadith grounds excellence in worship in awareness of Allah, including when the worshipper does not see Him.

questions.question: Quran 16:35 reports people using Allah's will to excuse their false worship. Read with 16:36, which conclusion follows?

options.text: If an act occurs, Allah must have commanded people to perform it.
The existence of divine will removes the purpose of messengers.
Human customs become revelation whenever many people follow them.
An appeal to divine will does not cancel the messengers' call to worship Allah and avoid false worship.

questions.explanation: The passage reports this excuse, then describes the messengers' command to worship Allah and reject false worship. Occurrence and religious command are not interchangeable.

questions.question: A speaker claims that knowing a little religious history gives them unrestricted knowledge of the unseen. Which evidence most directly challenges that claim?

options.text: Quran 6:59 places the keys of the unseen with Allah, and 72:26-27 describes disclosure to chosen messengers.
Knowledge of historical dates automatically establishes knowledge of all future events.
An audience's approval makes the speaker's predictions revelation.
Any statement about an unseen matter becomes true when repeated widely.

questions.explanation: These passages distinguish Allah's knowledge of the unseen from what He chooses to disclose. A person's religious knowledge does not establish unrestricted access to it.

questions.question: A person fears that Allah might overlook a small good deed or treat someone unjustly. Which response is supported by Quran 4:40?

options.text: Justice applies only to deeds that other people remember.
Allah does not wrong anyone even by a tiny amount, and He increases the reward of good.
Small good deeds have no place in divine judgment.
People must announce a good deed before Allah can know it.

questions.explanation: An-Nisa 4:40 affirms exact justice and generous reward for good. The verse connects accountability with Allah's fairness, not public recognition.

questions.question: Which statement about intercession is consistent with Quran 2:255?

options.text: An intercessor can overrule Allah's decision independently.
Human influence guarantees intercession regardless of Allah's permission.
No one can intercede with Allah except by His permission.
Intercession transfers Allah's final authority to someone else.

questions.explanation: Ayat al-Kursi places intercession under Allah's permission. It does not describe an independent power able to compel Him.

questions.question: Someone performs worship mainly to gain admiration. Which requirement in Quran 98:5 is most directly relevant to correcting the intention?

options.text: Obtaining the largest audience possible
Making every private action public
Measuring worship only by its outward appearance
Sincere devotion to Allah

questions.explanation: Al-Bayyinah 98:5 calls for sincere devotion to Allah alongside worship. Public visibility by itself does not establish sincerity.

questions.question: A person thinks they can guarantee another person's acceptance of faith through personal influence. Which distinction does Quran 28:56 establish?

options.text: A person cannot guarantee guidance for someone they love; Allah guides whom He wills.
Affection for someone guarantees their acceptance of every teaching.
Human persuasion gives a person control over other people's hearts.
The verse makes conveying a message identical to controlling its acceptance.

questions.explanation: Al-Qasas 28:56 addresses the limits of even the Prophet's control over another person's guidance. It distinguishes human desire from Allah's granting of guidance.

questions.question: Quran 2:253 mentions distinctions in favour among messengers, while 2:285 describes believers accepting all messengers. How can these teachings be understood together?

options.text: Differences in rank permit believers to reject messengers of a lower rank.
Allah may favour some messengers while believers still accept every messenger He sent.
Accepting every messenger means every messenger must have exactly the same rank.
A believer may accept only the messengers named in their own language.

questions.explanation: Accepting all messengers concerns their truthfulness and mission from Allah. This does not deny distinctions Allah Himself mentions among them.

questions.question: Which description of the Quran's relationship to earlier scripture most closely follows Quran 5:48?

options.text: It teaches that Allah never revealed any scripture before it.
It gives every later human opinion the same authority as revelation.
It confirms earlier scripture and serves as a criterion or guardian over it.
It says religious judgment should be based only on people's preferences.

questions.explanation: Al-Ma'idah 5:48 describes confirmation and oversight of earlier scripture and directs judgment by what Allah revealed. Translations use terms such as criterion, guardian or overseer.

questions.question: After a loss, one person falls into consuming despair; after success, another becomes boastful. What balance is taught in Quran 57:22-23?

options.text: Belief in decree requires the absence of all ordinary human sadness.
Every success proves permanent superiority over other people.
Every loss proves that beneficial effort was religiously forbidden.
Awareness of Allah's decree should temper excessive grief over losses and boastfulness over gains.

questions.explanation: The passage links prior decree with avoiding being overwhelmed by loss or becoming boastful over what is received. It does not demand emotional numbness.

questions.question: Someone treats religious belief as entirely unrelated to wishing good for others. Which teaching in Sahih al-Bukhari 13 challenges that separation?

options.text: The hadith connects faith with loving for one's brother what one loves for oneself.
The hadith makes concern for others depend only on shared wealth.
The hadith says outward success guarantees complete faith.
The hadith limits all religious responsibility to private feelings.

questions.explanation: The hadith links faith with sincere concern for another person's good. This tests the relationship between belief and conduct, not the judgment of a named individual's faith.

questions.question: In Quran 49:14, some people claim belief and are told to describe their submission instead. What distinction does the passage illustrate?

options.text: Human observers can always measure another person's inner faith perfectly.
An outward claim does not by itself establish that faith has entered the heart.
A person's tribal identity alone proves the completeness of faith.
Speaking a religious phrase automatically reveals every inner intention.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes a claim of belief from faith entering the heart in that specific address. It does not give quiz users a method for judging other people's hearts.

questions.question: A person says a child automatically carries a parent's moral guilt. Which response best follows Quran 6:164?

options.text: Moral guilt is inherited in the same way as property.
A child's moral responsibility is determined only by the parent's reputation.
A person does not bear another person's burden of sin.
Family membership prevents every person from being judged individually.

questions.explanation: The verse rejects transferring one person's burden to another. Family connections do not make a child personally guilty of a parent's act.

questions.question: A religious claim is widely shared online, but the speaker offers no knowledge or evidence for it. Which response best follows Quran 17:36?

options.text: Treat the number of shares as proof that the claim is revelation.
Repeat it confidently until someone disproves it.
Assume sincerity makes checking the claim unnecessary.
Do not assert it as established knowledge merely because it is popular.

questions.explanation: Al-Isra 17:36 warns against following what one has no knowledge of and connects hearing, sight and the heart with accountability.
